#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Spike: can the default GITHUB_TOKEN update a managed branch whose
# .github/workflows differ from main, via the GitHub commit API?
set -uo pipefail

R="$GITHUB_REPOSITORY"
MANAGED=managed
STAGING="$MANAGED--staging"
SUMMARY="${GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY:-/dev/stdout}"
PNG_B64='iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAYAAAAfFcSJAAAADUlEQVR42mNkYPhfDwAChwGA60e6kgAAAABJRU5ErkJggg=='

log() { printf '%s\n' "$*"; }
record() { printf '%s\n' "$*" >> "$SUMMARY"; printf 'RESULT %s\n' "$*"; }

git config user.name spike
git config user.email spike@example.com
git fetch --no-tags origin "+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*" >/dev/null 2>&1
BASE=$(git rev-parse origin/main)
PR=$(gh pr list --repo "$R" --head "$MANAGED" --state open --json number --jq '.[0].number // empty')
record "base main sha: $BASE; managed PR: #${PR:-none}"
record "workflows diverge (origin/managed...origin/main -- .github/workflows): $(git diff --stat "origin/$MANAGED...origin/main" -- .github/workflows | tail -1)"

with_token_remote() {
  git remote set-url origin "REDACTED"
}

case_A() {
  log "== A: regenerate from main, git push --force =="
  with_token_remote
  git switch -C regen "$BASE" >/dev/null 2>&1
  echo "1.2.0" > VERSION
  git commit -qam "regen"
  out=$(git push --force origin "HEAD:refs/heads/$MANAGED" 2>&1); code=$?
  record "A git push --force regenerated branch: exit=$code :: $(echo "$out" | grep -E 'rejected|refusing|->' | head -3 | tr '\n' ' ')"
  git switch -q --detach "$BASE"
}

case_B() {
  log "== B: git push --force main sha to managed =="
  with_token_remote
  out=$(git push --force origin "$BASE:refs/heads/$MANAGED" 2>&1); code=$?
  record "B git push --force <main sha>:managed: exit=$code :: $(echo "$out" | grep -E 'rejected|refusing|->' | head -3 | tr '\n' ' ')"
}

staging_at() {
  local sha="$1" out
  if out=$(gh api -X PATCH "repos/$R/git/refs/heads/$STAGING" -f sha="$sha" -F force=true 2>&1); then
    log "staging PATCH ok"
  else
    log "staging PATCH failed ($out); trying POST"
    gh api -X POST "repos/$R/git/refs" -f ref="refs/heads/$STAGING" -f sha="$sha" >/dev/null
  fi
}

delete_staging() { gh api -X DELETE "repos/$R/git/refs/heads/$STAGING" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true; }

build_local_tree() {
  # Working tree = base + intended changes; returns git write-tree oid.
  git switch -q --detach "$BASE"
  git reset -q --hard "$BASE"
  echo "$1" > VERSION
  git rm -q keep.txt
  printf 'line one\r\nline two\r\n' > crlf.txt
  printf '%s' "$PNG_B64" | base64 -d > pixel.png
  git add -A
  git write-tree
}

commit_payload() {
  # $1 version, $2 expectedHeadOid -> body.json
  jq -n \
    --arg repo "$R" --arg branch "$STAGING" --arg head "$2" \
    --arg version "$(printf '%s\n' "$1" | base64 -w0)" \
    --arg crlf "$(printf 'line one\r\nline two\r\n' | base64 -w0)" \
    --arg png "$PNG_B64" \
    '{query: "mutation($input: CreateCommitOnBranchInput!) { createCommitOnBranch(input: $input) { commit { oid } } }",
      variables: {input: {
        branch: {repositoryNameWithOwner: $repo, branchName: $branch},
        message: {headline: "chore(release): version packages (spike)"},
        expectedHeadOid: $head,
        fileChanges: {
          additions: [{path: "VERSION", contents: $version}, {path: "crlf.txt", contents: $crlf}, {path: "pixel.png", contents: $png}],
          deletions: [{path: "keep.txt"}]
        }}}}' > body.json
}

case_C() {
  local label="${1:-C}" version="${2:-1.1.0}"
  log "== $label: staging + createCommitOnBranch + updateRef(force) =="
  local_tree=$(build_local_tree "$version")
  staging_at "$BASE"
  commit_payload "$version" "$BASE"
  out=$(gh api graphql --input body.json 2>&1); code=$?
  new_sha=$(echo "$out" | jq -r '.data.createCommitOnBranch.commit.oid // empty' 2>/dev/null)
  if [[ $code -ne 0 || -z "$new_sha" ]]; then
    record "$label createCommitOnBranch FAILED exit=$code :: $(echo "$out" | head -c 600 | tr '\n' ' ')"
    delete_staging; return 1
  fi
  remote_tree=$(gh api "repos/$R/git/commits/$new_sha" --jq .tree.sha)
  verified=$(gh api "repos/$R/commits/$new_sha" --jq '.commit.verification.verified')
  reason=$(gh api "repos/$R/commits/$new_sha" --jq '.commit.verification.reason')
  author=$(gh api "repos/$R/commits/$new_sha" --jq '.commit.author.name')
  record "$label createCommitOnBranch ok: sha=$new_sha tree_equal=$([[ "$remote_tree" == "$local_tree" ]] && echo yes || echo NO) verified=$verified reason=$reason author=$author"
  out=$(gh api -X PATCH "repos/$R/git/refs/heads/$MANAGED" -f sha="$new_sha" -F force=true 2>&1); code=$?
  ref_now=$(gh api "repos/$R/git/refs/heads/$MANAGED" --jq .object.sha)
  record "$label updateRef(force) managed: exit=$code ref_now_matches=$([[ "$ref_now" == "$new_sha" ]] && echo yes || echo NO) :: $(echo "$out" | grep -io 'refusing[^"]*\|message[^,]*' | head -2 | tr '\n' ' ')"
  sleep 3
  state=$(gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$R" --json state --jq .state 2>/dev/null)
  files=$(gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$R" --json files --jq '[.files[].path] | sort | join(",")' 2>/dev/null)
  wf_diff=$(git fetch -q origin && git diff --name-only "origin/main...origin/$MANAGED" -- .github/workflows | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
  record "$label PR #$PR state=$state files=[$files] workflow_paths_in_pr_diff=$wf_diff"
  delete_staging
}

case_D() {
  log "== D: stale expectedHeadOid =="
  stale=$(git rev-list --max-parents=0 HEAD | tail -1)
  build_local_tree "1.1.0" >/dev/null
  staging_at "$BASE"
  commit_payload "1.1.0" "$stale"
  out=$(gh api graphql --input body.json 2>&1); code=$?
  record "D stale expectedHeadOid: exit=$code :: $(echo "$out" | jq -r '.errors[0].message // .message // empty' 2>/dev/null | head -c 300)"
  delete_staging
}

case_E() {
  log "== E: payload size probes =="
  for mib in 1 8 32; do
    staging_at "$BASE"
    contents=$(yes 'payload line for spike sizing 0123456789' | head -c $((mib*1024*1024)) | base64 -w0)
    jq -n --arg repo "$R" --arg branch "$STAGING" --arg head "$BASE" --arg c "$contents" \
      '{query: "mutation($input: CreateCommitOnBranchInput!) { createCommitOnBranch(input: $input) { commit { oid } } }",
        variables: {input: {branch: {repositoryNameWithOwner: $repo, branchName: $branch}, message: {headline: "size probe"}, expectedHeadOid: $head, fileChanges: {additions: [{path: "big.txt", contents: $c}]}}}}' > big.json
    out=$(gh api graphql --input big.json 2>&1); code=$?
    sha=$(echo "$out" | jq -r '.data.createCommitOnBranch.commit.oid // empty' 2>/dev/null)
    record "E ${mib}MiB: exit=$code ok=$([[ -n "$sha" ]] && echo yes || echo NO) :: $(echo "$out" | jq -r '.errors[0].message // .message // empty' 2>/dev/null | head -c 200)$( [[ -z "$sha" && $code -ne 0 ]] && echo "$out" | grep -v '^{' | head -c 200)"
    rm -f big.json
    delete_staging
  done
}

case_F() {
  log "== F: rerun C twice with identical content =="
  case_C "F1" "1.1.0"
  case_C "F2" "1.1.0"
}

run_case() {
  case "$1" in
    A) case_A ;; B) case_B ;; C) case_C ;; D) case_D ;; E) case_E ;; F) case_F ;;
    all) case_A; case_C; case_D; case_F; case_E; case_B ;;
    *) echo "unknown case $1"; exit 2 ;;
  esac
}

run_case "$CASE"
record "done"

  # Working tree = base + intended changes; returns git write-tree oid.
  git switch -q --detach "$BASE"
  git reset -q --hard "$BASE"
  echo "$1" > VERSION
  git rm -q keep.txt
  printf 'line one\r\nline two\r\n' > crlf.txt
  printf '%s' "$PNG_B64" | base64 -d > pixel.png
  git add -A
  git write-tree
}

commit_payload() {
  # $1 version, $2 expectedHeadOid -> body.json
  jq -n \
    --arg repo "$R" --arg branch "$STAGING" --arg head "$2" \
    --arg version "$(printf '%s\n' "$1" | base64 -w0)" \
    --arg crlf "$(printf 'line one\r\nline two\r\n' | base64 -w0)" \
    --arg png "$PNG_B64" \
    '{query: "mutation($input: CreateCommitOnBranchInput!) { createCommitOnBranch(input: $input) { commit { oid } } }",
      variables: {input: {
        branch: {repositoryNameWithOwner: $repo, branchName: $branch},
        message: {headline: "chore(release): version packages (spike)"},
        expectedHeadOid: $head,
        fileChanges: {
          additions: [{path: "VERSION", contents: $version}, {path: "crlf.txt", contents: $crlf}, {path: "pixel.png", contents: $png}],
          deletions: [{path: "keep.txt"}]
        }}}}' > body.json
}

case_C() {
  local label="${1:-C}" version="${2:-1.1.0}"
  log "== $label: staging + createCommitOnBranch + updateRef(force) =="
  local_tree=$(build_local_tree "$version")
  staging_at "$BASE"
  commit_payload "$version" "$BASE"
  out=$(gh api graphql --input body.json 2>&1); code=$?
  new_sha=$(echo "$out" | jq -r '.data.createCommitOnBranch.commit.oid // empty' 2>/dev/null)
  if [[ $code -ne 0 || -z "$new_sha" ]]; then
    record "$label createCommitOnBranch FAILED exit=$code :: $(echo "$out" | head -c 600 | tr '\n' ' ')"
    delete_staging; return 1
  fi
  remote_tree=$(gh api "repos/$R/git/commits/$new_sha" --jq .tree.sha)
  verified=$(gh api "repos/$R/commits/$new_sha" --jq '.commit.verification.verified')
  reason=$(gh api "repos/$R/commits/$new_sha" --jq '.commit.verification.reason')
  author=$(gh api "repos/$R/commits/$new_sha" --jq '.commit.author.name')
  record "$label createCommitOnBranch ok: sha=$new_sha tree_equal=$([[ "$remote_tree" == "$local_tree" ]] && echo yes || echo NO) verified=$verified reason=$reason author=$author"
  out=$(gh api -X PATCH "repos/$R/git/refs/heads/$MANAGED" -f sha="$new_sha" -F force=true 2>&1); code=$?
  ref_now=$(gh api "repos/$R/git/refs/heads/$MANAGED" --jq .object.sha)
  record "$label updateRef(force) managed: exit=$code ref_now_matches=$([[ "$ref_now" == "$new_sha" ]] && echo yes || echo NO) :: $(echo "$out" | grep -io 'refusing[^"]*\|message[^,]*' | head -2 | tr '\n' ' ')"
  sleep 3
  state=$(gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$R" --json state --jq .state 2>/dev/null)
  files=$(gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$R" --json files --jq '[.files[].path] | sort | join(",")' 2>/dev/null)
  wf_diff=$(git fetch -q origin && git diff --name-only "origin/main...origin/$MANAGED" -- .github/workflows | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
  record "$label PR #$PR state=$state files=[$files] workflow_paths_in_pr_diff=$wf_diff"
  delete_staging
}

case_D() {
  log "== D: stale expectedHeadOid =="
  stale=$(git rev-list --max-parents=0 HEAD | tail -1)
  build_local_tree "1.1.0" >/dev/null
  staging_at "$BASE"
  commit_payload "1.1.0" "$stale"
  out=$(gh api graphql --input body.json 2>&1); code=$?
  record "D stale expectedHeadOid: exit=$code :: $(echo "$out" | jq -r '.errors[0].message // .message // empty' 2>/dev/null | head -c 300)"
  delete_staging
}

case_E() {
  log "== E: payload size probes =="
  for mib in 1 8 32; do
    staging_at "$BASE"
    contents=$(yes 'payload line for spike sizing 0123456789' | head -c $((mib*1024*1024)) | base64 -w0)
    jq -n --arg repo "$R" --arg branch "$STAGING" --arg head "$BASE" --arg c "$contents" \
      '{query: "mutation($input: CreateCommitOnBranchInput!) { createCommitOnBranch(input: $input) { commit { oid } } }",
        variables: {input: {branch: {repositoryNameWithOwner: $repo, branchName: $branch}, message: {headline: "size probe"}, expectedHeadOid: $head, fileChanges: {additions: [{path: "big.txt", contents: $c}]}}}}' > big.json
    out=$(gh api graphql --input big.json 2>&1); code=$?
    sha=$(echo "$out" | jq -r '.data.createCommitOnBranch.commit.oid // empty' 2>/dev/null)
    record "E ${mib}MiB: exit=$code ok=$([[ -n "$sha" ]] && echo yes || echo NO) :: $(echo "$out" | jq -r '.errors[0].message // .message // empty' 2>/dev/null | head -c 200)$( [[ -z "$sha" && $code -ne 0 ]] && echo "$out" | grep -v '^{' | head -c 200)"
    rm -f big.json
    delete_staging
  done
}

case_F() {
  log "== F: rerun C twice with identical content =="
  case_C "F1" "1.1.0"
  case_C "F2" "1.1.0"
}

run_case() {
  case "$1" in
    A) case_A ;; B) case_B ;; C) case_C ;; D) case_D ;; E) case_E ;; F) case_F ;;
    all) case_A; case_C; case_D; case_F; case_E; case_B ;;
    *) echo "unknown case $1"; exit 2 ;;
  esac
}

run_case "$CASE"
record "done"

My harness script has a shell bug: GitHub Actions always runs `run:` blocks with `bash -e`, and `out=$(git push ...); code=$?` triggers `errexit` on the assignment itself when `git push` fails, aborting the script *before* `code=$?` or any of my error-printing ever runs. content.text: `createCommitOnBranch` works fine for non-workflow paths, and the restriction is specifically scoped to `.github/workflows/*` paths in the commit itself — exactly matching the git-push restriction, and exactly what the plan predicted. name: spike-push-test
on:
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: write

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          persist-credentials: false
      - name: staging commit (no workflow paths) then move a workflow-stale branch's ref
        run: |
          R="${{ github.repository }}"
          BASE=$(git rev-parse origin/main)
          STALE="spike/relpr-stale-managed"
          STAGING="spike/relpr-updateref-staging"

          set +e
          gh api -X POST "repos/$R/git/refs" -f ref="refs/heads/$STAGING" -f sha="$BASE" >/dev/null 2>&1
          set -e

          jq -n --arg repo "$R" --arg branch "$STAGING" --arg head "$BASE" \
            --arg content "$(printf 'non-workflow content %s\n' "$(date +%s)" | base64 -w0)" \
            '{query: "mutation($input: CreateCommitOnBranchInput!) { createCommitOnBranch(input: $input) { commit { oid } } }",
              variables: {input: {
                branch: {repositoryNameWithOwner: $repo, branchName: $branch},
                message: {headline: "spike: staging commit, no workflow paths"},
                expectedHeadOid: $head,
                fileChanges: {additions: [{path: "spike-nonworkflow-target.txt", contents: $content}]}
              }}}' > body.json

          set +e
          out=$(gh api graphql --input body.json 2>&1)
          code=$?
          set -e
          echo "$out" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          new_sha=$(echo "$out" | jq -r '.data.createCommitOnBranch.commit.oid // empty' 2>/dev/null)
          printf 'RESULT createCommitOnBranch (staging, no workflow paths) exit=%s new_sha=%s\n' "$code" "${new_sha:-none}" | tee -a "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

          if [[ -n "$new_sha" ]]; then
            set +e
            move_out=$(gh api -X PATCH "repos/$R/git/refs/heads/$STALE" -f sha="$new_sha" -F force=true 2>&1)
            move_code=$?
            set -e
            printf 'RESULT updateRef(force) on workflow-stale branch exit=%s :: %s\n' "$move_code" "$move_out" | tee -a "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

            after_sha=$(gh api "repos/$R/git/refs/heads/$STALE" --jq '.object.sha' 2>/dev/null)
            printf 'RESULT stale branch ref now=%s matches_new_sha=%s\n' "$after_sha" "$([[ "$after_sha" == "$new_sha" ]] && echo yes || echo no)" | tee -a "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

            has_wf=$(gh api "repos/$R/contents/.github/workflows/spike-push-test.yml?ref=$STALE" 2>&1 | jq -r 'if .message then "absent" else "present" end' 2>/dev/null)
            printf 'RESULT stale-branch-only workflow file now: %s (expect absent = inherited from main successfully)\n' "$has_wf" | tee -a "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          fi

          set +e
          gh api -X DELETE "repos/$R/git/refs/heads/$STAGING" >/dev/null 2>&1
          set -e
          exit 0

content.text:
Found it precisely. Public repos enforce this restriction; private repos don't (at least on this org/plan tier). `orin-dx/callisto` is public. Confirmed with a clean, isolated, brand-new **public** throwaway repo — same setup as before, and it reproduced the exact rejection verbatim:

```
RESULT push exit=1 ::  ! [remote rejected] HEAD -> managed (refusing to allow a GitHub App to create or update workflow `.github/workflows/dummy.yml` without `workflows` permission)
```

So the full, now-verified picture:
1. **Root cause**: on public repos, `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot write to `.github/workflows/*` — not via `git push`, not via `createCommitOnBranch`'s own `fileChanges`. Confirmed directly on `orin-dx/callisto` (public) twice, and reproduced cleanly in an isolated public throwaway repo. This explains the original `33679599559` failure completely — nothing repo-specific or mysterious, just public-repo policy.
2. **The proposed fix works**: a commit built via `createCommitOnBranch` that touches only non-workflow paths, staged at current `main`'s tip, then moved onto the real branch via a plain REST `updateRef` — **succeeded on the real, public `orin-dx/callisto` repo**, confirmed directly, including verifying the target branch's `.github/workflows` subtree became byte-identical to `main`'s. The ref move itself isn't treated as "creating or updating a workflow file" — only a direct write to that path is.

So: simple push doesn't work (confirmed on the real repo, twice), and the `createCommitOnBranch` + `updateRef` design from the plan does work (confirmed on the real repo, once, precisely). This isn't theoretical anymore — Phase 0 spike is GO, on solid ground.

Cleaning up all the spike repos/branches now, then I'll continue with implementation per the approved plan.

attachment.content:
- courier:changeset: Trigger when the user asks to add a changeset or document a change: "add a changeset", "document this change", "what changed here". Extracts the consumer-facing meaning of a diff: classifies consumer_impact (behavior-change, new-capability, internal-only) and semver_impact (major, minor, patch, none) per shared/references/changesets.md's decision table, then writes a summary scaled to that classification. A diff spanning multiple independent topics — common on a backlog/catch-up run, not just a single PR — produces one changeset per topic, not one bundled entry. When the change came via smith, pass along implementer's criteria_evidence — changeset-analyzer uses those exact locations instead of reconstructing approximate ones from the diff.
- courier:commit: Trigger when the user asks to commit code or write a commit message: "commit this", "write a commit message", "commit the staged changes". Reads the staged git diff and produces a conventional commit message explaining why the change was made, not what changed — the diff already shows what changed.
- courier:post-review: Trigger when the user has an already-drafted review or reply and wants it posted: "post this review", "reply to this comment", "mark this thread resolved", "submit my review comments". Takes drafted content — from the built-in `code-review` skill's findings, from `courier/receive-feedback`'s response plan, or typed directly by the user — and posts it to GitHub via `gh pr review` or `gh pr comment`. Does not draft content itself; this skill is purely mechanical execution of something already written, gated by explicit user confirmation before any post fires.
- courier:pr: Trigger when the user asks to open a PR or write a PR description: "open a PR", "create a pull request", "write the PR description". Given a diff, a linked spec, and a linked requirement, produces a PR title and body a reviewer with zero context can act on, then opens the PR via `gh pr create` after user confirmation.
- courier:receive-feedback: Trigger when the user asks to process or triage incoming review feedback: "address the feedback", "respond to review comments", "what do these comments mean", "triage this review". Assembles a review package — diff summary, linked spec, test results, open questions — so the author has full context to respond without re-reading the whole thread. Does not categorize individual comments by priority; that's the caller's judgment call, made with `shared/references/github.md`'s vocabulary in hand. This is for feedback received on the user's own PR — critiquing someone else's PR is the built-in `code-review` skill's job, not this one.
- courier:release: Trigger when the user asks to cut a release or summarize what's in one: "cut a release", "what's in this release", "generate release notes". Aggregates changeset@2 entries since the last release into a release-artifact@2: filters consumer_impact: internal-only entries, computes the version as max(semver_impact) across the rest applied to the prior version, and carries each changeset's summary through unedited.
- muse:component: Trigger when the user asks to spec a UI component: "spec this component", "draft a component spec", "write a spec for this design", "audit this component spec", "is this component spec ready?", "gate this component spec". Given a requirement@1 or free-text design intent, produces a spec@1 covering props, variants, per-state observable behavior, and accessibility criteria as testable propositions. Every criterion is falsifiable from outside the implementation; error cases and invalid prop combinations carry is_error_case: true. No TBDs anywhere in the document — genuinely unknown items go in non_goals or the reasoning scratchpad instead. Gated by a binding exit gate before the spec proceeds to planning.
- navigator:plan: Trigger this skill when the user says "write a plan for X", "how do we implement this spec", "break this down into tasks", "what are the implementation steps", "create an implementation plan", or "plan this out". Also activate when a spec (spec@1) exists and the user is ready to move to implementation but hasn't broken it down yet. Produces a plan@1 artifact where every task includes exact file paths, a brief implementation approach, exact implementation code, the exact tests proving each criterion, a conventional commit message, and covers_criteria linking the task to specific acceptance criteria. spec_file_path and linked_requirement are propagated from the source spec. No TBDs. No "implement as appropriate." Every step is mechanically executable by a developer with zero domain context.
- ranger:audit: Trigger this skill when the user asks to perform a bug hunt, code audit, find bugs, security audit, defect scan, vulnerability scan, code review for bugs, or asks "what's wrong with this code." Activate for any codebase language — Rust, TypeScript, or JavaScript. 5-phase pipeline: (1) recon builds a verified module manifest and detects the primary language; (2) scanner reads language-specific hazard taxonomies and emits candidates in live files only; (3) boundary-tracer (conditional) traces field survival for T7/T10 candidates; (4) adversary refutes each candidate by tracing control flow — unrebutted candidates survive as confirmed (concrete failing scenario stated) or plausible (no refutation, but reachability depends on state outside the code); (5) exit-gate re-reads code from scratch, verifies confirmed findings are resolved, checks sibling gaps, confirms compile/tests pass, carries plausible findings forward for human review without blocking on them, and escalates after 3 failed retries. Never reports bugs in dead or unreachable code. Output follows finding-report@1.
- scribe:architect: Trigger when ranger has returned a finding-report@1 and the confirmed defect class needs a structural fix — a change to the architecture, type system, interface boundary, or abstraction layer — rather than patches to individual instances. Given a finding-report@1, produces a spec@1 for the structural change that makes the defect class impossible or unrepresentable, not merely documented or harder to introduce. Acceptance criteria must be falsifiable at the type or API level.
- scribe:audit-architecture: Trigger when a draft spec@1 needs checking against the workspace's whole-system architecture — not another spec, and not a single signature — before it reaches scribe/gate-spec: "check this spec against our architecture", "does this fit the system", "audit this against the arch model". Given a spec@1, checks it against the persisted arch-model@1 for boundary violations, competing abstractions, and invariant conflicts, building or refreshing the model first if it's absent or stale for the area the spec touches. Returns specific, rewritten fixes on fail, the same standard as scribe/audit-spec but at system scope instead of spec scope.
- scribe:audit-spec: Trigger when the user asks to review a spec's quality: "review this spec", "is this spec complete?", "audit this spec". Given a spec@1, adversarially reviews it for untestable criteria, ambiguous language, missing error cases, scope overlap with other specs, and incomplete sections. Returns a structured issue list with specific rewritten suggested fixes, not generic guidance. Named audit-spec rather than audit because the bare word audit is already ranger's plugin-level skill name (code/bug auditing) — a different domain entirely.
- scribe:correct-spec: Trigger when implementer reports that a spec criterion contradicts what the system actually does: a spec_contradiction status from smith. Given a spec_file_path, the criterion_id of the affected acceptance criterion, and a contradiction report (what the spec says vs. what the system actually does), revises the affected criterion — and any criteria that depend on it — and returns a corrected spec@1 with revision_note set. Use this when implementation reveals the spec itself is wrong, not merely hard to satisfy.
- scribe:draft-spec: Trigger when the user asks to write or draft a spec: "spec this out", "draft a spec", "write a spec for this requirement". Given a requirement@1 and optionally a research-report@1, produces a spec@1 draft with purpose, scope, non_goals, api_surface (if applicable), and acceptance criteria. Every criterion is a testable proposition; error cases carry is_error_case: true. No TBDs anywhere in the document — genuinely unknown items go in non_goals or the reasoning scratchpad instead.
- scribe:gate-spec: Trigger when a spec@1 needs a definitive pass/fail judgment before it enters planning: "gate this spec", "is this spec ready?", "check this spec before we plan it". Default disposition is fail — the spec must earn a pass. Passes only if every acceptance criterion is testable with no vague language, no TBDs remain, error cases are explicitly covered, and scope is narrow enough for one planning cycle. This gate checks the spec on its own terms — whole-system architectural fit is scribe/audit-architecture's job upstream, not re-litigated here. On fail, returns blockers specific enough for scribe/draft-spec to act on without further clarification.
- scribe:spec-drift: Trigger when the user asks whether implemented code still matches its spec, weeks or months after implementation: "check spec drift", "does the code still match this spec?", "has this spec drifted?". Given a spec@1 (via spec_file_path) and a workspace root, reads the spec from disk and the implementation from the workspace, and reports each criterion as covered (implemented and tested), uncovered (no matching implementation), or drifted (implementation exists but diverges from the criterion's contract). This is an on-demand diagnostic, not a blocking gate — scribe/gate-spec is the blocking gate.
- scribe:verify-spec: Trigger when the user asks whether a spec matches its source: "is this grounded?", "does this spec match the requirement?", "check this spec against the requirement". Given a draft spec@1 plus the originating requirement@1 and optional research-report@1, checks whether each acceptance criterion is grounded in the source artifacts. Classifies criteria as supported, unsupported, or overfitted. Collects evidence only — does not produce a pass/fail verdict. Use before implementation, not after — for post-implementation drift, use scribe/spec-drift instead.
- sentinel:gate: Trigger this skill when the user says "verify this", "check this spec", "check this plan", "check this requirement", "check this PR", "is this done?", "review this for completeness", "does this meet the criteria?", "gate this", or "quality check" — also before stage transitions: starting implementation from a spec, shipping from an implementation, opening a PR from a branch. Applies to any stage artifact: requirements, specs, plans, implementations, PRs. Do not activate for general Q&A, code explanation, or exploratory work with no artifact boundary being crossed. The gate either clears the artifact for the next stage or returns specific, actionable blockers to the producing agent.
- smith:implement: Activate when the user says "implement this", "execute the plan", "write the code", "build this feature", "generate tests for X", "write tests for this spec", "refactor this without changing behavior", or "explain what this code does" — also when handed a plan@1 to execute, or a spec@1 exists but no plan. Every task: design the approach, write the implementation and comprehensive tests proving the covers_criteria, confirm the full suite passes, commit. Mutation testing then verifies the test suite would catch real faults — not a write-test-first ordering — surviving mutants return to the implementer as precision tests before the exit gate runs. The sentinel exit gate verifies all spec criteria independently at the end, reading the codebase from scratch and assuming the implementation is incomplete. Works from plan@1 (preferred) or spec@1 directly.
- vanguard:research: Activate when the user says "I need to understand X before deciding", "is there a way to do Y", "what are the options for Z", "research this", "investigate this", "what does the codebase already do for X", "prior art on Y", or "what are the risks of approach Z" — also when the approach for a spec or plan is unclear, when checking what dependencies exist for a feature, or when any design question needs an evidence base before commitment. Investigates the question across internal sources (specs, docs, codebase patterns, manifests) and external sources as needed, then produces a research-report@1 that distinguishes confirmed findings from likely inferences from unverified assumptions, with a falsifiable recommendation and explicit confidence level so a spec writer (scribe) isn't surprised by implementation reality.
- weaver:audit-backlog: Trigger when the user asks about overall backlog health: "what's in the backlog", "audit the backlog", "what requirements are missing coverage". Cross-references all open requirement@1 objects against existing specs and implementation files. Returns per-requirement status (covered, partial, missing, duplicate) with evidence, plus a structured summary — per-status counts and an optional one-clause note, not a prose paragraph. Named audit-backlog rather than bare audit because that word is already ranger's plugin-level skill name (code/bug auditing) — a different domain entirely.
- weaver:capture-need: Trigger when the user describes a raw need in free text: "we need X", "the problem is Y", "users are asking for Z". Converts unstructured text into a structured requirement@1 draft — id, statement, stakeholder, why, done_when — without asking clarifying questions. Fields that cannot be inferred are omitted, not fabricated. out_of_scope is intentionally left empty for weaver/connect-requirement or a human to fill in.
- weaver:clarify-requirement: Trigger when a requirement@1 draft from weaver/capture-need has gaps to close before a spec can be written: "is this requirement complete?", "what's missing from this requirement". Given a requirement@1, evaluates gaps in priority order — testability of done_when, specificity of stakeholder, explicitness of out_of_scope — and either asks one focused question or returns the completed requirement with out_of_scope populated. One question per invocation, never a list.
- weaver:connect-requirement: Trigger when the user asks whether a specific requirement already exists or relates to other work: "is this already captured?", "does this overlap with an existing requirement?", "what does this relate to?". Given one requirement@1 (or a small named set), searches the workspace for related specs and implementation files, and checks for duplicate or overlapping requirements. Returns coverage status and duplicate_of references scoped to just the requirement(s) given — not a full backlog sweep.
- weaver:prioritize-backlog: Trigger when the user asks what to work on first from a set of requirements: "what should we prioritize", "rank the backlog", "what's most urgent". Given a list of requirement@1 drafts, ranks them by impact, urgency, and dependency order — a requirement another depends on ranks above the one depending on it, even if its own impact/urgency score is lower. Returns an ordered list with a concrete rationale per requirement.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.

input.name: specs-docs-changesets
input.description: Update specs, plan, docs, changesets for Phase 5
input.prompt:
You are documenting an already-fully-designed, already-approved architecture change to the Rust project Callisto. Work in the git worktree /tmp/callisto-relpr-debug-specs, on branch feat/release-pr-api-commit-specs (already checked out there — don't switch branches, don't touch main, don't push). This worktree is a sibling checkout of the same repo as /tmp/callisto-relpr-debug, where a separate agent is concurrently implementing the actual Rust/shell code on branch feat/release-pr-api-commit — you must NOT touch any code files (crates/, .github/actions/, .github/workflows/, Justfile) since that would conflict; your job is exclusively .claude/specs/, .claude/plans/, docs/, ARCHITECTURE.md, and .changeset/.

## Background
Callisto's GitHub composite action maintains a long-lived "release PR" branch by regenerating it from current `main` and `git push --force-with-lease`-ing it with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`. On a PUBLIC GitHub repository (confirmed empirically against the real orin-dx/callisto repo, not theoretical), that token cannot write to `.github/workflows/*` through the Git push protocol OR through GitHub's GraphQL `createCommitOnBranch` mutation's own `fileChanges`, on any ref — this was proven with real, reproducible test runs, including one exact production failure: `refusing to allow a GitHub App to create or update workflow '.github/workflows/callisto-ci.yml' without 'workflows' permission` (GitHub Actions run 33679599559, 2026-09-02). The prior mitigation closed the stale PR and opened a fresh SHA-suffixed one whenever the base branch's workflow files had moved since the branch was cut (a `Supersede` decision) — this caused real user-visible PR churn (#28 closed, #48 opened) that the maintainer wants gone, without adding a privileged PAT/token.

The fix, empirically verified against the real repo: build a commit via `createCommitOnBranch` that touches ONLY non-workflow paths (so `.github/workflows/*` is inherited unchanged from the commit's parent, never written to), staged on a deterministic branch rooted at the current base commit, then move the real managed branch's ref onto that new commit via a plain REST ref update (`PATCH .../git/refs/heads/<branch>`) — a ref move is not itself a write to `.github/workflows/*` and is not subject to the restriction, confirmed directly: `createCommitOnBranch` with only non-workflow changes succeeded on the real repo, and the subsequent `updateRef(force)` onto a branch whose `.github/workflows` differed from the new commit's inherited content also succeeded, with the target branch's `.github/workflows` subtree ending up byte-identical to `main`'s.

## What is actually shipping (implemented by the other agent, you are documenting it)
- `crates/callisto-model/src/release_pr.rs`: `ReleasePrSnapshotV1`/`ReleasePrActionV1`/`ReleasePrDecisionV1` (schema version 1) are replaced by `ReleasePrSnapshotV2`/`ReleasePrActionV2`/`ReleasePrDecisionV2` (schema version 2). `ReleasePrPullRequestV1`'s `workflow_delta_from_base: bool` field is replaced by `ReleasePrPullRequestV2`'s `head_commit: CommitSha`. `ReleasePrActionV2` has three variants: `Noop{reason}`, `Create{branch, staging_branch}`, `Update{pull_request_number, branch, expected_head_commit, staging_branch}` — `Supersede` is gone entirely, no replacement, no runtime fallback. `staging_branch` is deterministic: `"{release_branch}--staging"` (via `ReleasePrConfigV1::staging_branch()`). `verify_snapshot` now also catches a moved PR head commit (via `head_commit`), which is the compare-and-swap surrogate for the executor's non-atomic REST ref update. A brand new `ReleasePrCommitPlanV1` (schema version 1) type with `from_changes(base_commit, message, Vec<StagedChangeV1>)` builds the exact typed `createCommitOnBranch` payload (`additions[{path, contentsBase64}]`, `deletions[{path}]`) from a Git index diff — it fails closed (new error codes E149-E154) on: an empty change set, any non-regular-file Git mode (executable bit, symlink, submodule — `createCommitOnBranch`'s GraphQL schema cannot express modes at all, only plain 100644 blobs), renames/copies/type-changes/unmerged paths, any `.github/workflows/*` or otherwise unsafe path (`.git/`, `..`, absolute, NUL), and a payload over a conservative 4 MiB cap (`MAX_COMMIT_PLAN_BYTES`, unmeasured against GitHub's real limit — a sizing spike hit a client-tooling bug rather than a clean measurement, so this is deliberately conservative headroom over today's real ~150-200 KB payload, not a validated ceiling). `managed_branch_shape` still accepts the canonical branch or a `--<40-hex-sha>` suffixed branch (so the existing PR #48, on `callisto/version-packages--567f321c8cae20c66ab7bf90ca59d493978c84b0`, remains a recognized managed branch and gets updated in place going forward — it is not migrated or renamed).
- `crates/callisto-vcs`: a new `ShellGit::staged_changes_since(base) -> Vec<StagedChangeV1>` observation (git diff --cached --raw parsing + reading worktree bytes), exposed through `GitAccess`.
- `crates/callisto-cli`: a new read-only `callisto release-pr commit-plan --base-commit <sha> --message <msg> [--out <file>]` subcommand.
- `.github/actions/callisto-action/scripts/create-or-update-release-pr.sh`: rewritten executor — no `git push` anywhere. Snapshot collection drops the per-PR `git fetch`/workflow-diff loop (now just `gh pr list --json number,headRefName,headRepository,headRefOid`). Sequence: decide -> compose PR body -> run the version command -> `git add -A` -> `callisto release-pr commit-plan` -> compare `git write-tree` against the API commit's tree SHA (byte-fidelity check) -> `release-pr verify` (x3, before staging, before the real ref move, and again before PR writes) -> stage the commit via GraphQL `createCommitOnBranch` on the deterministic staging branch -> move the real branch's ref via REST `PATCH .../git/refs/heads/<branch>` (or `POST` for create) -> the existing label/PR create-or-edit logic, unchanged -> a trap that always deletes the staging ref.
- `.github/workflows/callisto-release.yml`: the `version-pr` job's checkout flips to `persist-credentials: false` (it never runs `git push` anymore, so it needs no persisted git credentials — only `GH_TOKEN` for `gh` calls, which it already had).
- `.github/actions/callisto-action/action.yml`: `setup_git_user` input is kept (backward-compatible) but is now a documented no-op — there is no local git commit/push step left for it to configure identity for.

## Your tasks

1. **`.claude/specs/SPEC-RELEASE-PR-DECISION-014.json`** (currently status "draft"): Read it first. Update `architecture.execution` to describe materializing the change via the forge commit API from a Callisto-built commit plan, the staging branch, and the tree-equality check — replace the current "version from the current base, commit/push the selected branch" language, since there is no local git push anymore. Update AC-002 (drop the "unless its observed workflow delta requires supersede" clause — supersede no longer exists; zero eligible managed PRs still yields create, exactly one still yields update, more than one still fails closed, and add that a PR on the reserved staging branch itself fails closed too). Update AC-003 (replace the supersede-branch-naming criterion with the commit-plan contract: the commit's parent is always the snapshot's base commit, it never contains a `.github/workflows/*` path, non-regular file modes and renames/copies/type-changes are refused, and the SHA-suffixed replacement branches created by the old supersede behavior remain valid, updatable managed branches going forward — they are not migrated away from). Update AC-004's test list (the black-box contract tests now demonstrate create, update, retained `--sha`-suffixed replacement branch update, no-op, stale-snapshot refusal before any mutation, a moved PR head caught before the ref move, a tree-mismatch refusal, staging-branch cleanup on failure, and that the script never invokes `git push` — remove references to a supersede test). Add a new acceptance criterion (AC-006) for the `commit-plan` contract itself: parent is always the snapshot base commit, forbidden-path/mode/kind refusals are typed and tested, byte-fidelity is provable via a `git write-tree` comparison. Bump AC-005's schema reference to v2. Add a `revision_note` explaining this revision, citing the empirical findings above (the production failure on run 33679599559, and the direct confirmation on the real repo that `createCommitOnBranch` + a plain ref move succeeds where `git push` does not). Leave `status` as "draft" unless you have strong reason to change it — that's the implementer's call, not yours.

2. **`.claude/specs/SPEC-RELEASE-INTERFACES-013.json`**: Read it first, focusing on the acceptance criterion around line 40 that currently describes "If GitHub's built-in token rejects updating that long-lived managed branch because the base branch has changed a workflow since it diverged, the flow automatically creates a SHA-suffixed replacement managed branch and PR..." — replace that sentence with something like: the flow updates the managed branch through the forge commit API (never a local `git push`) specifically so the built-in token never needs to write `.github/workflows/*` on any ref; a branch that was already replaced under the old supersede behavior (a `--<sha>` suffix) remains a trusted, ordinary managed branch and continues to be updated in place. Keep the surrounding sentences about "recomputes rather than rebasing" and "requires no elevated token" — those are still true and still load-bearing, don't remove them. Add a brief `revision_note`.

3. **New `.claude/plans/PLAN-RELEASE-PR-API-COMMIT-015.json`**: Follow the exact JSON shape of the existing `.claude/plans/PLAN-RELEASE-PR-DECISION-014.json` (read it first for the schema: artifact_type, schema, id, status, goal, specs[], steps[] each with id/kind/description/verify[]/commit, final_acceptance). Steps: T00 (the empirical spike — describe what was tested and found, with an `evidence` field summarizing the concrete run/test results above, marked complete/GO), T01 (model types — already committed, mark complete), T02 (VCS staged_changes_since), T03 (CLI commit-plan subcommand), T04 (action script + workflow rewrite + test suites), T05 (this spec/doc/changeset work you're doing right now). Reference SPEC-RELEASE-PR-DECISION-014.json as the linked spec.

4. **`docs/06-publishing.md`**: Read the "Repository durable-release workflow" section (roughly lines 15-25) first. Replace the paragraph describing the supersede/SHA-suffixed-branch/optional-PAT behavior with a description of the forge-commit-API approach: no local git push, commits are GitHub-signed ("Verified") and attributed to `github-actions[bot]`, the built-in token needs no `workflows` permission because it's never asked to write that path, and — for repositories that keep an already-superseded `--<sha>` branch from before this change — that branch is still a normal, continuously-updated managed branch, not something requiring migration.

5. **`ARCHITECTURE.md`**: Read the relevant section first (search for "GitHub-token fallback" and the `release_branch`/action input table, roughly section 9 and around line 407). content.text:
# Fewer Permission Prompts

Look through my transcripts' MCP and bash tool calls, and based on those, make a prioritized list of patterns that I should add to my permission allowlist to reduce permission prompts. Focus on read-only commands.

The format for permissions is: `Bash(foo*)`, `Bash(foo)`, `Bash(foo bar *)`, `mcp__slack__slack_read_thread`, etc.

Then, add these to the project `.claude/settings.json` under `permissions.allow`.

## Steps

1. **Locate transcripts.** Session transcripts live at `~/.claude/projects/<sanitized-cwd>/*.jsonl`. Each line is a JSON object. Tool calls appear as `assistant` messages with `message.content[]` entries of `type: "tool_use"`. The `name` field identifies the tool (e.g. `"Bash"`, `"mcp__slack__slack_read_thread"`); for Bash, `input.command` is the shell string.

   Scan the recent transcripts across the user's projects dir — not just the current project — so the allowlist reflects their actual usage. Cap the scan at a reasonable number of recent sessions (e.g. 50 most-recently-modified JSONL files) so this stays fast.

2. **Extract tool-call frequencies.**
   - For `Bash` calls: parse `input.command`, take the leading command token (handling `sudo`, `timeout`, pipes, `&&`, env-var prefixes). Record the command + first subcommand pair (e.g. `git status`, `gh pr view`, `ls`, `cat`).
   - For MCP calls: record the full tool name (e.g. `mcp__slack__slack_read_thread`).
   - Count occurrences across the scanned transcripts.

3. **Filter to read-only.** Keep only commands that don't mutate state. Examples of read-only: `ls`, `cat`, `pwd`, `git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`, `git branch`, `rg`, `grep`, `find`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`, `file`, `which`, `echo`, `date`, `gh pr view`, `gh pr list`, `gh pr diff`, `gh issue view`, `gh issue list`, `gh run list`, `gh run view`, `gh api` (GET), `bun run typecheck`, `bun run lint`, `bun run test` (for tests that don't mutate), `docker ps`, `docker logs`, `kubectl get`, `kubectl describe`, `ps`, `top`, `df`, `du`, `env`, `printenv`, any MCP tool with `read`/`get`/`list`/`search`/`view` in its name.

   Drop anything that writes, deletes, renames, pushes, merges, installs, or runs a build/test that has side effects. When in doubt, leave it out.

   **Never allowlist a pattern that grants arbitrary code execution.** A wildcard rule for any of these (e.g. `Bash(python3:*)`) is equivalent to allowing arbitrary code execution. This list is not exhaustive — apply the same rule to anything in the same category:
   - Interpreters: `python`/`python3`, `node`, `bun`, `deno`, `ruby`, `perl`, `php`, `lua`, etc.
   - Shells: `bash`, `sh`, `zsh`, `fish`, `eval`, `exec`, `ssh`, etc.
   - Package runners: `npx`, `bunx`, `uvx`, `uv run`, etc.
   - Task-runner wildcards: `npm run *`, `yarn run *`, `pnpm run *`, `bun run *`, `make *`, `just *`, `cargo run *`, `go run *`, etc. — an exact `Bash(bun run typecheck)` is fine, `Bash(bun run *)` is not
   - `gh api *`, `docker run`/`exec`, `kubectl exec`, `sudo`, and similar

4. **Drop commands Claude Code already auto-allows.** These don't need an allowlist entry — they never prompt. If you see any of these in the transcripts, skip them; don't suggest them to the user.

   - **Always auto-allowed (any args):** `cal`, `uptime`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`, `stat`, `strings`, `hexdump`, `od`, `nl`, `id`, `uname`, `free`, `df`, `du`, `locale`, `groups`, `nproc`, `basename`, `dirname`, `realpath`, `cut`, `paste`, `tr`, `column`, `tac`, `rev`, `fold`, `expand`, `unexpand`, `fmt`, `comm`, `cmp`, `numfmt`, `readlink`, `diff`, `true`, `false`, `sleep`, `which`, `type`, `expr`, `seq`, `tsort`, `pr`, `echo`, `ls`, `cd`.
   - **Auto-allowed with zero args only:** `pwd`, `whoami`, `alias`.

import json, re

files = [l.strip() for l in open('/tmp/recent_transcripts.txt') if l.strip()]

gh_api_examples = Counter()
just_examples = Counter()

for fp in files:
    try:
        with open(fp, 'r', errors='ignore') as f:
            for line in f:
                line = line.strip()
                if not line: continue
                try: obj = json.loads(line)
                except Exception: continue
                msg = obj.get('message', {})
                content = msg.get('content')
                if not isinstance(content, list): continue
                for item in content:
                    if not isinstance(item, dict) or item.get('type') != 'tool_use': continue
                    if item.get('name') != 'Bash': continue
                    cmd = item.get('input', {}).get('command', '')
                    if not cmd: continue
                    if re.search(r'\bcargo fmt\b', cmd) and len(fmt_examples) < 15:
                        fmt_examples.append(cmd[:100])
                    m = re.search(r'\brtk (\S+)', cmd)
                    if m:
                        rtk_examples[m.group(1)] += 1
                    if re.search(r'\bgh api\b', cmd):
                        # capture whether -X is used
                        mutating = bool(re.search(r'-X\s*(POST|PATCH|DELETE|PUT)', cmd, re.I))
                        gh_api_examples['mutating' if mutating else 'GET'] += 1
                    m2 = re.search(r'\bjust (\S+)', cmd)
                    if m2:
                        just_examples[m2.group(1)] += 1
    except Exception:
        pass

print("=== cargo fmt examples ===")

print("=== rtk subcommands ===")

print("=== gh api mutating vs GET ===")
for k,v in gh_api_examples.items(): print(v,k)
print("=== just subcommands ===")
for k,v in just_examples.most_common(20): print(v,k)
PYEOF

Write a PR title and body for the diff between origin/main and HEAD on branch feat/release-pr-api-commit in the git worktree /tmp/callisto-relpr-debug (repo orin-dx/callisto). Read the diff yourself: `cd /tmp/callisto-relpr-debug && git diff origin/main...HEAD` (25 files, +1575/-285across 5 commits — read `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD` for the commit sequence too). Linked spec: `.claude/specs/SPEC-RELEASE-PR-DECISION-014.json` (read it — it was updated in this same diff). Linked plan: `.claude/plans/PLAN-RELEASE-PR-API-COMMIT-015.json` (new in this diff, records the empirical spike evidence).

Context for your narrative, from the reviewer's perspective — write for someone with zero prior context on why this change exists:

The problem: Callisto's release-PR GitHub Action maintains one long-lived branch by regenerating it from current `main` and force-pushing with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`. On a public repository, that token cannot write to `.github/workflows/*` through the Git push protocol, on any ref — confirmed by an actual production failure (GitHub Actions run 33679599559 on orin-dx/callisto, 2026-09-02): `refusing to allow a GitHub App to create or update workflow '.github/workflows/callisto-ci.yml' without 'workflows' permission`. The prior mitigation closed the stale PR and opened a fresh SHA-suffixed one whenever the base branch's workflow files had moved since the branch was cut (a `Supersede` decision) — this produced real, unwanted PR churn (PR #28 closed, #48 opened) that the maintainer wanted eliminated without adding a privileged PAT/token.

The fix, empirically verified directly against the real orin-dx/callisto repo (not just theory, not just a throwaway sandbox repo — a public throwaway repo reproduced the same rejection, and the real repo was used for the final confirmation): GitHub's GraphQL `createCommitOnBranch` mutation also can't write `.github/workflows/*` with the default token, but a *ref move* onto a commit that inherits unchanged workflow content from its parent is not itself treated as a write to that path. So the new executor stages a commit containing only non-workflow changes via `createCommitOnBranch` on a deterministic `<release-branch>--staging` branch rooted at the current base commit, verifies the resulting commit's tree is byte-identical to a local `git write-tree` (proving fidelity — no silent mode/rename/encoding loss), then moves the real managed branch's ref onto that commit via a plain REST `PATCH .../git/refs/heads/<branch>`. This was confirmed to succeed on the real repo even when the target branch's `.github/workflows` differed from the new commit's inherited content.

What shipped, one commit per phase:
1. `feat(model)`: `ReleasePrSnapshotV2`/`ReleasePrActionV2`/`ReleasePrDecisionV2` replace the v1 types (schema version bump 1→2). `Supersede` and the `workflow_delta_from_base` field are removed entirely — no replacement, no runtime fallback. `ReleasePrActionV2::Update`/`Create` now carry a deterministic `staging_branch`; `Update` also carries `expected_head_commit`, the compare-and-swap surrogate for the executor's non-atomic REST ref move (`verify_snapshot` now catches a moved PR head). New `ReleasePrCommitPlanV1::from_changes()` builds the exact typed `createCommitOnBranch` payload from a Git index diff, failing closed (6 new error codes) on non-regular file modes (executable bit, symlink, submodule — the GraphQL schema can't express modes at all), renames/copies/type-changes/unmerged paths, any `.github/workflows/*` or otherwise unsafe path, an empty change set, or a payload over a conservative 4 MiB cap.
2. `feat(vcs)`: `ShellGit::staged_changes_since()` — observes a Git index diff against a base commit and reads worktree bytes for additions/modifications.
3. `feat(cli)`: new read-only `callisto release-pr commit-plan --base-commit <sha> --message <msg> [--out <file>]` subcommand; `release-pr decide`/`verify` moved onto the v2 types.
4. `feat(action)`: the executor script rewritten with zero `git push` calls anywhere; the `version-pr` job's checkout drops `persist-credentials: true` (no longer needed since there's no local git push); both action test suites rewritten — the stub contract test now covers the full staging/commit/ref-move/cleanup sequence including failure paths (stale snapshot, moved PR head, tree mismatch, staging cleanup on failure), and the real-binary contract test (which actually compiles and calls the compiled `callisto` binary rather than stubbing it, specifically because a prior incident showed a stubbed-JSON contract test cannot catch a real serialization bug) now also exercises `commit-plan`'s exact jq→GraphQL mapping.
5. `docs`: specs/plan/docs/changesets updated to match (separate commit, produced in parallel in a sibling worktree, merged in).

Existing SHA-suffixed managed branches (e.g. the live PR #48 on `callisto/version-packages--567f321c...`) remain valid, continuously-updated managed branches under the new code — they are not migrated or renamed, `managed_branch_shape` still accepts them.

Test plan for the PR body: cite that `cargo test --workspace`, `just ci-fast`, and both `.github/actions/callisto-action/tests/*.sh` suites were run and passed on the merged branch (I verified this myself independently, not just trusting agent self-reports) — write this as a reviewer-actionable checklist per the PR template in shared/references/github.md, not just prose.

Output a JSON object with title, body, labels, and your reasoning scratchpad, per your normal contract.

- Replace the release-PR executor's local `git push` (which the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot use to write `.github/workflows/*` on any ref) with a forge-API sequence: stage non-workflow changes via GraphQL `createCommitOnBranch` on a deterministic `<branch>--staging` branch rooted at the base commit, verify the resulting tree is byte-identical to a local `git write-tree`, then move the real managed branch's ref with a plain REST `PATCH .../git/refs/heads/<branch>`.
- Drop the `Supersede` decision and `workflow_delta_from_base` entirely (schema v1 -> v2 `ReleasePrSnapshot`/`Action`/`Decision` types) -- no replacement, no runtime fallback -- since it only masked the token-permission problem by cutting a fresh SHA-suffixed PR whenever workflow files drifted on `main`.
- Add supporting building blocks: `ReleasePrCommitPlanV1::from_changes` (fails closed on workflow paths, non-regular file modes, renames, and oversized payloads), `ShellGit::staged_changes_since`, and a new `callisto release-pr commit-plan` CLI subcommand.

## Why
On a public repo, the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot write `.github/workflows/*` through the Git push protocol -- confirmed by a real production failure (GitHub Actions run 33679599559 on orin-dx/callisto, 2026-09-02): `refusing to allow a GitHub App to create or update workflow '.github/workflows/callisto-ci.yml' without 'workflows' permission`. The prior mitigation (`Supersede`: close the stale PR, open a fresh SHA-suffixed one) worked around the symptom and produced unwanted churn (PR #28 closed, #48 opened) every time a workflow file moved.

This was fixed by testing directly against the real `orin-dx/callisto` repo (a public throwaway repo first reproduced the rejection, then the real repo confirmed the fix), not by inference from docs: `createCommitOnBranch` is restricted the same way as `git push` for `fileChanges`, but a **ref move onto a commit that inherits unchanged workflow content from its parent** is not itself treated as a write to that path. So the executor now only ever commits non-workflow changes, and moves the branch pointer separately. `expected_head_commit`/tree checks make the non-atomic REST ref move safe against a race or fidelity loss.

Existing SHA-suffixed managed branches from the old behavior (e.g. `callisto/version-packages--567f321c...`, PR #48) are not migrated -- `managed_branch_shape` still recognizes and updates them in place.

## Breaking Changes
- `callisto-model`: `ReleasePrSnapshotV1`, `ReleasePrActionV1`, `ReleasePrDecisionV1`, and `ReleasePrPullRequestV1::workflow_delta_from_base` are removed with no compatibility shim, replaced by v2 equivalents. `ReleasePrActionV2` has no `Supersede` variant. Ships as a minor bump per the crate's pre-1.0 changeset policy, but any external consumer of these types must migrate.

## Test Plan
- [ ] `cargo test --workspace` passes on the merged branch
- [ ] `just ci-fast` passes on the merged branch
- [ ] `test_release_pr_contract.sh` passes -- create/update/retained-`--sha`/no-op/stale-snapshot/moved-head/tree-mismatch/staging-cleanup, and asserts no `git push`
- [ ] `test_release_pr_decide_binary_contract.sh` passes -- real binary, not a stub, including `commit-plan`'s jq->GraphQL mapping
- [ ] `ReleasePrCommitPlanV1::from_changes` refusal tests cover workflow path / executable-symlink-submodule mode / rename-copy-type-change / empty / oversized
- [ ] `callisto-release.yml`'s `version-pr` job no longer sets `persist-credentials: true`

## Related

**The merge commit itself is unsigned:**
```json
{"author":"github-actions[bot]","committer":"Gabe Castro","parents":["a1f1ebcc..."],"reason":"unsigned","verified":false}
```

One parent (a squash/rebase-style commit, not a two-parent merge), and the **committer is your own identity, not GitHub's**. That's the signature of a merge done by pushing locally (checkout, merge/rebase, `git push`) rather than through GitHub's own merge button or `gh pr merge` — a commit GitHub itself creates server-side always comes back signed and verified, regardless of merge strategy.

The `release-candidate` job correctly found PR #48 as the merged, matching release PR (that part passed — `prs == 1`), but its second, deliberate check failed: `verified == true`. Its own code comment states the intent directly: *"a trusted merge must be both an actual merge of the managed PR and a GitHub-verified signed commit. It cannot be a direct push."* That's a real trust boundary from the release-trust spec work, not a bug — it's specifically designed to reject exactly this: someone locally pushing something onto `main` that merely looks like the release PR's merge, bypassing GitHub's own record of the merge event. So `plan`/`build`/`execute` correctly stayed skipped.

content.text:
Technically yes — but I'd want to be direct about what you'd be giving up before touching it.

The `verified == true` check exists specifically to rule out a scenario the PR-association check alone doesn't fully close: a token or bot with `contents: write` on `main` pushing a commit directly (bypassing PR review entirely) that happens to superficially match the merged-PR pattern. Only GitHub's own merge/squash mechanism produces a signature it can verify — that's the actual thing distinguishing "a real review-then-merge happened" from "someone with push access manufactured matching content." Removing the check means: from now on, *any* push to `main` matching the branch-name pattern can trigger a real crates.io/npm publish, regardless of whether it went through review at all.

The thing is — you don't actually need to weaken it permanently to solve today's problem. Now that rebase-merge is disabled, every future legitimate squash-merge *will* come back signed, so the check will never produce another false negative like this one going forward. It only matters for this one already-merged, unsigned commit.

Two better-scoped options than a blanket removal:

1. **Revert-and-redo** (what I described before) — no pipeline change at all, just gets a fresh signed merge for the same content.
2. **A one-time, explicit manual override**: add a `workflow_dispatch` input to the Durable release workflow (e.g. `override_commit`) that lets a human explicitly assert "treat this specific commit as the release candidate," bypassing the signature check *only* when a person deliberately typed that SHA in — not a standing weakening of the default push-triggered path. This is a real (small) code/spec change, not a config toggle, so it'd need its own review too.

If you want speed over process, (2) is faster to use today but is a permanent addition to the codebase (once built, it stays); (1) touches nothing but takes an extra PR cycle. Which way do you want to go?

Good point, and that changes the calculus — this isn't just about our own repo's merge settings anymore, it's about what the action can promise to *every* repo that uses it. Not every consumer can guarantee GitHub-signed merges (some don't use squash-only, some route merges through third-party merge-queue tools that don't produce GitHub's own signature, some organizations disable it entirely).

Given that, I don't think the right fix is removing the check — it's making it **configurable per-repo** rather than hardcoded: a new action input (e.g. `require_verified_merge_commit`, defaulting to `true`) that a repo can explicitly opt out of if it can't guarantee signed merges, with the PR-association check (`prs == 1`, base/head match) remaining mandatory either way as the floor. Default stays strict for repos like ours that can meet it; repos that can't, opt out with eyes open to the reduced provenance guarantee, documented plainly in the spec so it's a deliberate choice, not a silent gap.

That's a real trust-boundary change across `SPEC-RELEASE-INTERFACES-013`/`SPEC-RELEASE-TRUST-010`, not a quick toggle — it needs the same rigor as everything else here (spec update, action input, tests for both branches of the flag). Worth scoping as its own piece of work separate from fixing today's stuck release.

Two independent decisions in front of you now:
1. **This specific stuck 0.6.0 release** — still open (revert-and-redo, or a scoped one-time manual override).
2. **Making the verified-commit requirement configurable for other repos** — a real feature, worth its own spec/plan.

Fair, and re-judging against that bar changes things a lot — most of these names actually pull real weight once you look closely (each word maps to an actual technical/security property), and I was wrong to flatten them:

- "ephemeral intent" — tells you intent is never persisted/cached, a real property from the spec.
- "intent-bound source tree" — tells you the build is deterministically tied to a specific verified intent, not built from arbitrary state.
- "verify same-run handoff *before credentials*" — tells you the ordering guarantee (handoff verified before secrets become available).
- "attest *declared* binary artifacts" — specific about what gets attested vs. what doesn't.
- "verify environment protection" / "require environment reviewers" — literally names the GitHub feature being checked.

None of that is filler — cutting it would make the Actions UI less informative, not cleaner. That's the opposite of what you asked for.

The one that's actually empty is the top-level workflow title: **"Durable release"**. "Durable" is a quality claim, not a description of what happens — it doesn't tell a reader anything the job names below it don't already say better. That's the real AI-slop instance here: an abstract-sounding adjective standing in for saying anything concrete.

Revised, much narrower proposal: rename just the workflow itself, `Durable release` → `Release` (matching the plain, concrete style of the sibling `Callisto CI & Validation` workflow and the file's own name, `callisto-release.yml`). Leave every job and step name as-is.

Correction — I was wrong to call it meaningless. There IS a real contrast: it's defined across `SPEC-RELEASE-PLAN-DURABILITY-001A/B/C` and `PLAN-RELEASE-REARCHITECTURE-008-013`. The **non-durable** version is the workflow's own prior design: a single job that computed the release plan *inline*, in the same shell block that pushed tags and published — the plan lived only as an in-memory/shell-variable value for one step and was gone the instant that step ended, with no way for a human to review it before it took effect.

"Durable" specifically means: the release intent is captured as an explicit, persisted, versioned artifact that survives the boundary between an *unprivileged* plan job and a *privileged* execute job — that's literally what makes the human-approval gate (the `environment: release` reviewer step) possible at all. If the plan were computed inline like before, there'd be nothing concrete to review or gate; it'd already be done.

So it's real, deliberately chosen, and documented — just documented in the specs, not anywhere a reader glancing at the GitHub Actions tab would ever see it. That's a different problem than "meaningless jargon": it's a real term of art used with zero on-the-spot explanation in its only user-facing appearance.

Given that, I'd still rename the *workflow title* to `Release` — a one-line UI label has no room to carry that nuance regardless of whether the concept is real, and "durable" alone reads as an unexplained adjective there. But I'd leave every actual mention of "durable" in the specs/docs alone, since that's exactly where the term is properly defined and where it's doing real work. Same call as before, just for the right reason this time — want me to make that one rename?
